0.1.goal: Summarise one class's 30 test scores two ways: describe the class you have, then infer a plausible range for the wider group.
0.1.question: A maths teacher has the end-of-term scores of her 30 students on her desk. She has two questions: how did my class do, and what can I say about similar students I never tested? We have the 30 scores, and we will answer the first question by describing and the second by inferring.

blocks.title: Enter the 30 test scores
blocks.text: The teacher's 30 end-of-term scores, held in a NumPy array. The mean is 74 and the standard deviation about 12.3, as in the lesson.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

scores = np.array([41,57,61,62,62,62,65,65,68,68,70,72,72,73,73,75,75,76,77,77,78,79,80,84,86,86,88,95,95,98])

print('students:', len(scores))
print('lowest to highest:', scores.min(), 'to', scores.max())
explain: Load NumPy, the library for lists of numbers, under the short name np so we can type np. instead of numpy.
Load SciPy's statistics tools; we need them in step 3 for the confidence interval.
Store the 30 scores in an array, so one command can work on all of them at once.
Print how many scores we have. Always check n first, because everything later depends on it.
Print the lowest and highest score, to see how far the results stretch before we compute anything.
blocks.meaning: 30 students, with scores from 41 to 98. That is a wide spread, so one average will hide differences between students. This is why we measure the spread as well as the centre in the next step.

blocks.title: Describe: summarise what we have
blocks.text: Descriptive statistics only talk about these 30 students. The mean and median give the centre, and the standard deviation (ddof=1, the sample version) gives the typical distance from the average.
blocks.code:
mean = scores.mean()
median = np.median(scores)
sd = scores.std(ddof=1)

print(f'mean   = {mean:.1f}')
print(f'median = {median:.1f}')
print(f'sd     = {sd:.1f}')
print(f'about 2/3 of scores lie within {mean - sd:.1f} to {mean + sd:.1f}')
explain: The mean (add all scores, divide by 30) is the balance point of the class and our headline answer to 'how did we do?'.
The median is the middle score after sorting. We compute it too, to see whether a few extreme scores are pulling the mean.
Standard deviation, the typical distance of a score from the mean. ddof=1 divides by n - 1, because a sample under-estimates the spread of its whole group.
Print the mean. The f-string puts the number inside the text, and :.1f rounds it to one decimal place.
Print the median on the next line so we can compare it with the mean.
Print the standard deviation, the number that says how far scores typically sit from the average.
Mean plus and minus one SD marks the range where about two thirds of bell-shaped scores fall: a picture of a typical student.
blocks.meaning: The mean and the median are both 74.0, so the class is balanced and no extreme scores drag the average. The SD of 12.3 means a typical student sits about 12 points from 74, and about two thirds of the scores fall between 61.7 and 86.3. These are plain facts about these 30 students.

blocks.title: Infer: a 95% confidence interval
blocks.text: Now treat the 30 students as a sample from a bigger group. stats.t.interval gives a range of plausible values for that group's true mean. The standard error (sd divided by the square root of n) says how much a mean of 30 scores wobbles.
blocks.code:
n = len(scores)
se = sd / np.sqrt(n)

low, high = stats.t.interval(0.95, df=n - 1, loc=mean, scale=se)

print(f'standard error = {se:.2f}')
print(f'95% CI for the true mean: ({low:.1f}, {high:.1f})')
explain: Store n, the number of scores. len() counts them, and we need n for both the standard error and the degrees of freedom.
Standard error = sd / square root of n. It says how much a mean of 30 scores would wobble from one sample to the next.
stats.t.interval builds a 95% range for the true mean. It uses the t distribution because we estimated the spread from the sample, with df = n - 1.
Print the standard error to two decimals, so we can see how precise our mean is.
Print the two ends of the interval: the low and high values of the true mean that fit our data.
blocks.meaning: The standard error is 2.24, so a mean of 30 scores like these would typically wobble by about 2 points. The 95% interval is 69.4 to 78.6. If these students are a fair sample of a wider group, that group's true average plausibly lies in this range. The 74.0 is only our best single guess.

blocks.title: What each one tells you
blocks.text: The describing numbers are exact facts about these 30 scores. The interval is an estimate about people we did not test, and it comes with stated uncertainty. That is the whole difference between the two branches.
blocks.code:
print('DESCRIBE: this class averaged', round(mean, 1), 'with a typical spread of', round(sd, 1))
print('INFER: a wider group of similar students probably averages between', round(low, 1), 'and', round(high, 1))
print('Is the interval narrower than the spread of scores?', (high - low) < 2 * sd)
explain: Print the descriptive statement. It is a fact about these 30 students only, so it carries no uncertainty.
Print the inferential statement. It is about students we did not test, so we give a range instead of one number.
Compare the interval's width with 2 SDs. The interval is much narrower, because it locates the average, not individual students.
blocks.meaning: True: the interval is about 9 points wide, far narrower than the roughly 25 points over which individual scores spread. Do not mix them up. The standard deviation describes how students differ, while the interval says where the group's average probably lies.

explain: Store the 30 scores in a vector called scores. c() is R's way of combining values into one list.
mean() adds the scores and divides by 30, giving the class average.
median() gives the middle score after sorting, a check against extreme scores.
sd() is the sample standard deviation (it divides by n - 1), the typical distance from the mean.
t.test(scores) runs a t-test, but we only want $conf.int from it: the 95% interval for the true mean.
r.expect: mean 74; median 74; sd 12.29; 95 percent confidence interval: 69.41 to 78.59
r.read: Four results appear: 74, 74 and 12.29 describe this class (mean, median, SD). The last line prints the interval 69.41 to 78.59, followed by attr(,"conf.level") 0.95. That interval is the inference about the wider group.
r.note: sd() in R is the sample version (divides by n - 1), the same as ddof=1. t.test(scores) is used here only to get the 95% interval for the mean.

spss.syntax:
DATA LIST FREE / score.
BEGIN DATA
41 57 61 62 62 62 65 65 68 68 70 72 72 73 73 75 75 76 77 77 78 79 80 84 86 86 88 95 95 98
END DATA.
EXAMINE VARIABLES=score
  /PLOT=NONE
  /STATISTICS=DESCRIPTIVES
  /CINTERVAL 95.
explain: Tell SPSS we type the data inside the syntax, in free format, into one variable called score.
BEGIN DATA marks where the data lines start.
The 30 scores, separated by spaces. SPSS reads them in order, one per case.
END DATA marks where the data end, and the full stop finishes the command.
EXAMINE is SPSS's Explore command, which gives detailed descriptive statistics for the variable score.
Switch the plots off, so that the output is only tables.
Ask for the Descriptives table: mean, median, standard deviation and the confidence interval.
Set the confidence level to 95%, the usual choice, and end the command with a full stop.
spss.read: Open the Descriptives table. Mean 74.00, Median 74.00 and Std. Deviation 12.29 describe the class. The row '95% Confidence Interval for Mean' shows a Lower Bound of 69.41 and an Upper Bound of 78.59: that is the inference.
spss.note: The Descriptives table shows the mean with its 95% confidence interval, the median, the standard deviation, the minimum and the maximum together.

stata.code:
clear
set obs 30
generate score = real(word("41 57 61 62 62 62 65 65 68 68 70 72 72 73 73 75 75 76 77 77 78 79 80 84 86 86 88 95 95 98", _n))
summarize score, detail
ci means score
explain: Remove any old data from memory, so that we start from a clean sheet.
Create 30 empty rows, one for each student, ready to hold the scores.
Fill score row by row: word() picks the n-th number from the text, and real() turns it into a number. A short way to enter 30 values.
summarize with detail prints the mean, the median (the 50% row), the standard deviation and more.
ci means gives the mean with its standard error and 95% confidence interval.
stata.read: In the summarize output, Mean 74 and the 50% row (the median) 74 describe the class, and Std. Dev. 12.29 is the typical spread. ci means then prints Mean 74, Std. err. 2.24 and a 95% interval of 69.41 to 78.59: the inference.
stata.note: The word() line is a compact way to type 30 numbers. summarize, detail gives the mean, median (the 50% row) and standard deviation (sample version). ci means gives the mean with its 95% confidence interval.

0.1.conclusion: The class averaged 74 with a typical spread of about 12 points: that is a plain fact about these 30 students. If they are a fair sample of similar students, the true average of that wider group plausibly lies between 69.4 and 78.6. Caution: that range is only trustworthy if the 30 students are representative of the group we want to talk about.

practice.scenario: A nurse measures the resting pulse (beats per minute) of 20 volunteers at a health fair. She wants to describe these 20 people, and also to estimate the average resting pulse of all adults who might come to such fairs.
tasks: Find the mean, median and sample standard deviation of the pulses.
Compute the standard error and a 95% confidence interval for the true mean.
Say which results describe the 20 volunteers and which one is an inference about all fair visitors.
practice.hint: Follow the lab's two branches: describe with mean, median and std(ddof=1), then infer with the standard error and stats.t.interval.

solution.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

pulse = np.array([64, 70, 72, 68, 75, 80, 66, 71, 74, 69, 77, 73, 62, 78, 72, 67, 70, 76, 65, 74])
n = len(pulse)
mean, sd = pulse.mean(), pulse.std(ddof=1)
se = sd / np.sqrt(n)
low, high = stats.t.interval(0.95, df=n - 1, loc=mean, scale=se)
print(f'n = {n}, mean = {mean:.1f}, median = {np.median(pulse):.1f}, sd = {sd:.2f}')
print(f'standard error = {se:.2f}')
print(f'95% CI: ({low:.1f}, {high:.1f})')
solution.answer: Mean 71.2, median 71.5 and sd 4.88: the volunteers sit about 5 beats from 71. The standard error is 1.09 and the 95% interval is 68.9 to 73.4. The first three numbers describe the 20 volunteers, while the interval infers the average of all fair visitors, assuming the volunteers are typical of them.

0.2.goal: Build a small student table with a nominal, an ordinal, a discrete and a continuous column, and see which summaries make sense for each.
0.2.question: A school office keeps a table of ten students with their eye colour, grade level, number of siblings and height. A new assistant wants to average every column. Which columns can we sensibly average, and what should we report for the others?

blocks.title: Build a table with four kinds of data
blocks.text: One column per type: eye colour (nominal), grade level (ordinal, so we tell pandas the order), siblings (discrete, counted) and height (continuous, measured). The dtypes show how pandas stores each one.
blocks.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    'eye': ['brown','blue','brown','green','brown','blue','hazel','brown','green','blue'],
    'grade': ['Sophomore','Senior','Freshman','Junior','Sophomore','Senior','Freshman','Sophomore','Junior','Senior'],
    'siblings': [1, 0, 2, 3, 1, 1, 0, 2, 4, 1],
    'height_cm': [172.4, 165.1, 180.3, 158.9, 175.6, 169.8, 162.2, 177.0, 171.3, 183.5],
})
df['eye'] = df['eye'].astype('category')
df['grade'] = pd.Categorical(df['grade'],
    categories=['Freshman','Sophomore','Junior','Senior'], ordered=True)
print(df.dtypes)
explain: Load pandas, Python's tool for tables of data, under the short name pd.
Start building a DataFrame (a table). Each entry below is one column, written as name: list of values.
Column eye: ten eye colours. They are names with no order, so the type is nominal.
Column grade: the school year. The years are ranked but the gaps are not equal, so the type is ordinal.
Column siblings: a count of brothers and sisters, so a discrete number.
Column height_cm: a measurement, where any value in a range is possible, so continuous.
Close the dictionary and the DataFrame call. Every opening bracket needs its partner.
Tell pandas that eye is a category. It then stops treating colours as free text and refuses arithmetic on them.
Turn grade into a category too, and start listing its order, because the order is what makes it ordinal.
Give the order Freshman to Senior and set ordered=True, so pandas can compare grades with each other.
Print the dtypes, a quick check that each column is stored as the kind of data we intended.
blocks.meaning: eye and grade are stored as categories, while siblings is a whole-number count (int64) and height_cm a measured decimal (float64). That is the first split of the lesson: two columns hold categories and two hold amounts. The next steps show why that matters.

blocks.title: Count the categories
blocks.text: For categories the natural summary is a count (or a percentage), not an average. value_counts does it. With sort=False the ordinal column stays in its natural order, from Freshman to Senior.
blocks.code:
print(df['eye'].value_counts())
print()
print(df['grade'].value_counts(sort=False))
print()
print('share Junior or above:', (df['grade'] >= 'Junior').mean())
explain: Count how many students have each eye colour. Counting is the natural summary for names.
Print an empty line to separate the tables.
Count each grade. sort=False keeps the natural order Freshman to Senior instead of ordering by size.
Print another empty line.
Compare each grade with Junior (allowed because grade is ordered). Taking the mean of True and False gives the share.
blocks.meaning: Brown is the most common eye colour (4 of 10), then blue (3), green (2) and hazel (1). The grades split into 2 Freshman, 3 Sophomore, 2 Junior and 3 Senior, and half the students (0.5) are Junior or above. For categories we report counts and shares, never an average.

blocks.title: Describe the numbers
blocks.text: Counts and measurements are real amounts, so mean, standard deviation and quartiles all make sense. describe gives them in one table.
explain: describe() gives the count, mean, standard deviation, minimum, quartiles and maximum of numerical columns. round(2) keeps it readable.
blocks.meaning: Students have 1.50 siblings on average (from 0 to 4, median 1) and an average height of 171.61 cm with a standard deviation of 7.88 cm. These summaries make sense because the values are real amounts: one more sibling or one more centimetre always means the same step.

blocks.title: Why averaging a category makes no sense
blocks.text: Pandas refuses to average a category. If you force it by turning grades into codes 1 to 4, you get a number like 2.6 that is not a grade, and it pretends the gaps between grades are equal. For an ordinal column use counts, the maximum or a share instead.
explain: Loop over the two category columns, to try the same operation on each of them.
try: attempt something that might fail, so that an error is caught and does not stop the whole program.
Ask for the column's mean. For categories pandas refuses, which is its way of saying the answer would be meaningless.
except TypeError: runs only if the attempt failed with that kind of error.
Report the refusal, putting the column name into the message.
Force it anyway: turn grades into codes 0 to 3, then add 1 to get 1 to 4.
Average the codes. It works as arithmetic, but the answer is not a grade and it pretends all the gaps are equal.
For an ordinal column a sensible summary is the highest category present.
blocks.meaning: Pandas refuses to average eye and grade. Forcing the grades into codes gives 2.6, which is not a grade and only means something if every step between grades were equal. Report counts or the highest grade present (Senior) instead.

r.code:
eye <- factor(c('brown','blue','brown','green','brown','blue','hazel','brown','green','blue'))
grade <- factor(c('Sophomore','Senior','Freshman','Junior','Sophomore','Senior','Freshman','Sophomore','Junior','Senior'),
  levels = c('Freshman','Sophomore','Junior','Senior'), ordered = TRUE)
siblings <- c(1, 0, 2, 3, 1, 1, 0, 2, 4, 1)
height_cm <- c(172.4, 165.1, 180.3, 158.9, 175.6, 169.8, 162.2, 177.0, 171.3, 183.5)
table(eye)
table(grade)
summary(siblings)
summary(height_cm)
mean(eye)
explain: Create eye as a factor, which is R's type for categories.
Create grade as a factor too. This line lists the ten grades, one per student.
levels gives the order from Freshman to Senior, and ordered = TRUE tells R the categories are ranked.
siblings is a plain numeric vector, because it is a count.
height_cm is a numeric vector too, because it is a measurement.
table(eye) counts the students in each eye colour.
table(grade) counts the students in each grade.
summary(siblings) prints the minimum, quartiles, mean and maximum of a numeric vector.
summary(height_cm) does the same for the heights.
Deliberately average a category. R refuses by returning NA with a warning, showing the result is meaningless.
r.expect: eye: blue 3, brown 4, green 2, hazel 1; grade: Freshman 2, Sophomore 3, Junior 2, Senior 3; siblings mean 1.5; height_cm mean 171.61; mean(eye) gives NA with a warning
r.read: table(eye) shows blue 3, brown 4, green 2, hazel 1, and table(grade) shows 2, 3, 2, 3. summary(siblings) gives a mean of 1.5 and summary(height_cm) a mean of 171.6. mean(eye) prints NA with a warning that the argument is not numeric or logical.
r.note: R lists the eye colours alphabetically, while pandas lists them by size. mean(eye) returns NA with a warning, R's way of refusing to average a category.

spss.menu: Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Frequencies (categories) and Descriptives (numbers)
spss.syntax:
DATA LIST FREE / eye (A6) grade siblings height.
BEGIN DATA
brown 2 1 172.4 blue 4 0 165.1 brown 1 2 180.3 green 3 3 158.9 brown 2 1 175.6
blue 4 1 169.8 hazel 1 0 162.2 brown 2 2 177.0 green 3 4 171.3 blue 4 1 183.5
END DATA.
VALUE LABELS grade 1 'Freshman' 2 'Sophomore' 3 'Junior' 4 'Senior'.
VARIABLE LEVEL eye (NOMINAL) /grade (ORDINAL) /siblings height (SCALE).
FREQUENCIES VARIABLES=eye grade.
DESCRIPTIVES VARIABLES=siblings height.
explain: Read the data typed below in free format. (A6) says eye is text of up to 6 characters, and the other columns are numbers.
BEGIN DATA starts the data lines.
Five students. Each one is written as eye colour, grade code, siblings and height, in that order.
The other five students. SPSS reads values in order, so where a line ends does not matter.
END DATA ends the data lines.
Attach names to the grade codes, so the output says Freshman instead of 1.
Tell SPSS each variable's measurement level: nominal, ordinal or scale. It then offers suitable choices.
Frequencies counts each category of eye and grade, which is the right summary for categories.
Descriptives gives the mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum, which suit the two numerical variables.
spss.read: The Frequencies tables show eye (blue 3, brown 4, green 2, hazel 1) and grade (Freshman 2, Sophomore 3, Junior 2, Senior 3) with percentages. The Descriptives table shows a Mean of 1.50 for siblings and 171.61 for height, with a height Std. Deviation of 7.88.
spss.note: SPSS stores grade as codes 1 to 4 with labels. VARIABLE LEVEL tells SPSS each column's measurement level; use Frequencies for the two categories and Descriptives for the two numbers.

stata.code:
clear
set obs 10
generate eye = word("brown blue brown green brown blue hazel brown green blue", _n)
generate grade = real(word("2 4 1 3 2 4 1 2 3 4", _n))
generate siblings = real(word("1 0 2 3 1 1 0 2 4 1", _n))
generate height = real(word("172.4 165.1 180.3 158.9 175.6 169.8 162.2 177.0 171.3 183.5", _n))
label define g 1 "Freshman" 2 "Sophomore" 3 "Junior" 4 "Senior"
label values grade g
tabulate eye
tabulate grade
summarize siblings height
explain: Clear any old data from memory.
Create ten empty rows, one for each student.
Make eye a text variable. word() takes the n-th word of the list for row n.
Make grade from the codes 1 to 4. real() turns each word into a number.
Make siblings the same way, as a number.
Make height the same way, as a number with decimals.
Define a set of labels called g that names the codes 1 to 4.
Attach the labels g to grade, so output shows Freshman to Senior instead of codes.
tabulate eye counts each eye colour, the right summary for names.
tabulate grade counts each grade, also with percentages.
summarize siblings height gives mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum, only for the two numerical variables.
stata.read: tabulate eye gives blue 3, brown 4, green 2, hazel 1, and tabulate grade gives 2, 3, 2, 3 with percentages. summarize shows siblings with a mean of 1.5 and height with a mean of 171.61 and a standard deviation of 7.88.
stata.note: Stata keeps the ordinal grade as codes 1 to 4 with value labels. tabulate counts categories, and summarize is for numbers only.

0.2.conclusion: Only siblings and height_cm can be sensibly averaged: 1.5 siblings and 171.6 cm. Eye colour (nominal) should be counted, and grade (ordinal) is best reported with counts, shares or the highest grade, since an average of 2.6 is not a grade. Caution: a column full of digits is not automatically an amount, so always ask what one step of one unit means.

practice.scenario: A librarian records 12 members: their membership type (student, staff or public), a satisfaction rating (Poor, OK, Good, Great), the books they borrowed last month and the minutes they spent per visit. She asks which summary suits each column.
tasks: Name the type of each of the four columns (nominal, ordinal, discrete or continuous).
Count the members per membership type and per rating, keeping ratings in order.
Find the share who rated Good or Great.
Describe the books and minutes columns.
practice.hint: Make a DataFrame, turn rating into an ordered Categorical, use value_counts for categories and describe() for the two numerical columns.

solution.code:
import pandas as pd

lib = pd.DataFrame({
    'member': ['student','staff','public','student','student','public','staff','student','public','student','staff','public'],
    'rating': ['Good','Great','OK','Good','Poor','Good','Great','OK','Good','Great','Good','OK'],
    'books': [3, 1, 0, 4, 2, 1, 5, 2, 0, 3, 1, 2],
    'minutes': [42.5, 25.0, 18.2, 55.1, 31.4, 22.8, 38.0, 47.3, 15.6, 60.2, 29.9, 33.3],
})
lib['rating'] = pd.Categorical(lib['rating'], categories=['Poor','OK','Good','Great'], ordered=True)
print(lib['member'].value_counts())
print(lib['rating'].value_counts(sort=False))
print('share Good or Great:', round((lib['rating'] >= 'Good').mean(), 2))
print(lib[['books', 'minutes']].describe().round(2))
solution.answer: Membership is nominal (student 5, public 4, staff 3) and rating is ordinal (Poor 1, OK 3, Good 5, Great 3), so 67% rated Good or Great. Books is discrete (mean 2.00) and minutes is continuous (mean 34.94, sd 14.16). Averages belong only to the last two columns.

0.3.goal: See that a sample statistic wanders around the fixed population parameter, that bigger samples wander less, and that a biased sample does not.
0.3.question: A university has 40,000 students and wants their average weekly study time, but it can only ask a few. Before trusting any sample, we must see how a sample mean behaves next to the true population mean. We start with a population small enough to see (ten shops' sales) and then use 10,000 simulated study times.

blocks.title: The lesson's ten shops
blocks.text: Here the population is small enough to see: monthly sales of 10 shops. The population mean (a parameter) is fixed. Each sample of 3 shops gives a different sample mean (a statistic). The population SD divides by N (ddof=0), the sample SD by n - 1 (ddof=1).
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

shops = np.array([12, 15, 9, 22, 18, 7, 25, 14, 20, 11])
mu = shops.mean()
print(f'population mean (mu) = {mu:.2f}, sigma = {shops.std(ddof=0):.3f}')

samples = {'A': shops[[0, 3, 5]], 'B': shops[[6, 4, 1]], 'C': shops[[2, 9, 7]]}
for name, s in samples.items():
    print(f'sample {name}: {s}  x-bar = {s.mean():.2f}  gap = {s.mean() - mu:+.2f}')
print(f'sample A sd = {samples["A"].std(ddof=1):.3f}')
explain: Load NumPy, the library for lists of numbers, as np.
Store the whole population: the monthly sales (in thousands) of all ten shops, so the truth is known exactly.
mu is the population mean. It is a parameter: one fixed number that never changes.
Print mu and sigma. ddof=0 divides by N, which is right because this is the whole population and not a sample.
Three samples of 3 shops each, picked by position. Python counts positions from 0.
Loop over the samples, taking the name and the values of each.
Show each sample's mean (a statistic) and its gap from mu. That gap is the sampling error.
Sample standard deviation with ddof=1: dividing by n - 1 makes up for a sample under-estimating the spread of the population.
blocks.meaning: The population mean mu is 15.30 and it never moves. The three samples give 13.67, 19.33 and 11.33, which are gaps of -1.63, +4.03 and -3.97. Each sample is honest, yet none hits 15.30. That miss is sampling error and it is normal. With only three shops, sample A's SD (7.638) can also be far from sigma (5.551).

blocks.title: A bigger, seeded population
blocks.text: Now a population of 10,000 weekly study times in hours, made with a fixed seed so everyone gets the same numbers. We pretend not to know its mean and compute it once: this is the parameter.
blocks.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
population = rng.normal(loc=14, scale=4, size=10_000).round(1)

mu = population.mean()
print('population size N =', len(population))
print(f'population mean mu = {mu:.3f}')
explain: Create a random number generator with seed 42. A fixed seed gives everyone the same 'random' numbers.
Make 10,000 weekly study times from a bell curve with mean 14 and SD 4, rounded to 0.1 hour. This is our pretend population.
Compute the population mean once. In real life it is unknown, here it is the target our samples aim at.
Print the population size N.
Print the population mean, our parameter.
blocks.meaning: The population holds 10,000 study times with a true mean of 13.959 hours. That is close to the 14 we aimed for, but not exactly 14, because even the population is one random draw. This fixed number is the parameter that every sample will try to hit.

blocks.title: Sampling error shrinks as n grows
blocks.text: For each sample size we draw one random sample and show its gap from mu. Then we repeat the draw 300 times to see the typical gap. Bigger samples miss by less. The gap never vanishes completely: that is sampling error, and it is normal.
blocks.code:
for n in [10, 50, 250, 1000]:
    one = rng.choice(population, size=n, replace=False).mean()
    many = [rng.choice(population, size=n, replace=False).mean() for _ in range(300)]
    typical = np.mean(np.abs(np.array(many) - mu))
    print(f'n = {n:4d}: one sample mean = {one:6.2f}, typical gap over 300 samples = {typical:.3f}')
explain: Try four sample sizes, from tiny to large.
Draw one random sample without replacement (nobody asked twice) and take its mean.
Repeat the draw 300 times to see the pattern of sample means, not just one lucky or unlucky sample.
Average the absolute gaps between those 300 sample means and mu. That is the typical sampling error.
Print the size, the one sample's mean and the typical gap.
blocks.meaning: The single sample means (12.40, 14.58, 14.04, 13.80) wander around 13.959. The typical gap shrinks as n grows: 1.066 at n = 10, 0.473 at 50, 0.203 at 250 and 0.098 at 1000. Using 25 times as many students cuts the error about five-fold. Bigger samples miss by less, but never by exactly zero.

blocks.title: A biased sample does not get better
blocks.text: Suppose we only ask the 1,000 heaviest studiers (say, people we meet in the library). Even with a large sample the mean stays far from mu, because the method is tilted. A bigger sample cannot fix bias.
blocks.code:
top = np.sort(population)[-1000:]

for n in [10, 100, 1000]:
    m = rng.choice(top, size=n, replace=False).mean()
    print(f'biased sample n = {n:4d}: mean = {m:.2f}, gap from mu = {m - mu:+.2f}')
explain: Sort the study times and keep the 1,000 highest: only the heaviest studiers, like asking only people in the library.
Try three sample sizes, again from small to large.
Draw a sample from that tilted group only, and take its mean.
Print the mean and its gap from the true mu, with a plus or minus sign.
blocks.meaning: All three means are around 21 hours, so the gaps from mu are +7.09, +6.83 and +7.09, whatever the sample size. A bigger sample shrinks random error but not bias, because the bias comes from who we ask. Choose fairly first, then make the sample large.

r.code:
shops <- c(12, 15, 9, 22, 18, 7, 25, 14, 20, 11)
mean(shops)
sqrt(mean((shops - mean(shops))^2))
A <- shops[c(1, 4, 6)]
mean(A)
sd(A)
mean(shops[c(7, 5, 2)])
mean(shops[c(3, 10, 8)])
explain: Store the population: the sales of all ten shops, in a vector.
mean(shops) is the population mean mu.
R's sd() divides by n - 1, so for sigma we average the squared gaps ourselves (dividing by N) and take the square root.
Sample A: shops number 1, 4 and 6. R counts positions from 1.
The mean of sample A is a statistic.
sd() of sample A is the sample standard deviation (n - 1), right for a sample.
Sample B: shops 7, 5 and 2, and its mean.
Sample C: shops 3, 10 and 8, and its mean.
r.expect: mu 15.3; population sigma 5.551; sample A mean 13.67, sd 7.638; sample B mean 19.33; sample C mean 11.33
r.read: R prints mu = 15.3 and sigma = 5.551, then sample A's mean 13.67 and SD 7.638, then 19.33 for sample B and 11.33 for sample C. The three statistics differ from each other and from 15.3, while mu stays put.
r.note: R, SPSS and Stata have no population SD command, so R uses the formula directly. Random draws would differ from Python's because each program has its own random numbers, so we use the lesson's fixed samples.

spss.syntax:

BEGIN DATA
12 1 15 0 9 0 22 1 18 0
7 1 25 0 14 0 20 0 11 0
END DATA.
DESCRIPTIVES VARIABLES=sales.
TEMPORARY.
SELECT IF (inA = 1).
DESCRIPTIVES VARIABLES=sales.
explain: Two variables: sales, and inA, which is 1 for shops in sample A and 0 for the others.
BEGIN DATA starts the data lines.
The first five shops, each written as a sales value and then its 1 or 0 marker.
The last five shops in the same pattern.
END DATA ends the data lines.
Descriptives of sales for all ten shops: the population summary.
TEMPORARY makes the next selection last for one command only, so the full data come back afterwards.
Keep only the shops with inA = 1, which is sample A.
Descriptives again, now for sample A alone.
spss.read: The first Descriptives table (N = 10) shows a Mean of 15.30, which is mu. Its Std. Deviation 5.851 is the sample version, not sigma 5.551. The second table (N = 3) shows Mean 13.67 and Std. Deviation 7.638: sample A's statistics.
spss.note: The first table shows mu = 15.3 for all 10 shops. The second, for sample A only, shows x-bar = 13.67 and SD 7.638. SPSS always gives the sample SD (n - 1), so for all 10 shops it shows 5.851, not the population 5.551.

Create ten empty rows, one per shop.
Fill sales from the text: word() picks the n-th number for row n and real() makes it numeric.
inA is 1 for rows 1, 4 and 6 (sample A) and 0 elsewhere. _n is the row number.
Summarize all ten shops, the population.
Summarize only the rows where inA equals 1, which is sample A.
stata.read: The first summarize shows 10 observations and a Mean of 15.3 (mu). Its Std. Dev. 5.851 uses n - 1. The second shows Obs 3, Mean 13.67 and Std. Dev. 7.638, the statistics of sample A, which differ from mu.
stata.note: The first summarize gives mu = 15.3 for all shops, the second gives x-bar = 13.67 and SD 7.638 for sample A. Stata's SD is always the sample version, so for all 10 shops it shows 5.851.

0.3.conclusion: A sample statistic is not the population parameter: it wanders around it by sampling error, as our three shop samples (13.67, 19.33, 11.33 against mu = 15.30) showed. Bigger samples wander less (typical gap 1.07 at n = 10 and 0.10 at n = 1000), but a biased way of choosing, such as asking only the heaviest studiers, stays about 7 hours off at any size.

practice.scenario: A landlord owns eight flats and knows the monthly electricity bill (in dollars) of every one. He wonders how well the mean of a small sample of flats would estimate the true mean of all eight, and whether asking more flats helps.
tasks: Find the population mean and the population standard deviation (ddof=0).
List every possible sample of 2 flats and of 5 flats (itertools.combinations) and compute each sample mean.
Compare the typical gap from mu for the two sample sizes, and the average of all sample means with mu.
practice.hint: itertools.combinations(bills, n) gives every way to pick n flats. Take np.mean of each, then compare np.abs(means - mu).mean().

solution.code:
import numpy as np
from itertools import combinations

bills = np.array([52, 61, 48, 75, 66, 58, 90, 54])
mu = bills.mean()
print(f'mu = {mu:.2f}, sigma = {bills.std(ddof=0):.2f}')
for n in [2, 5]:
    means = np.array([np.mean(c) for c in combinations(bills, n)])
    print(f'n = {n}: {len(means)} samples, average of sample means = {means.mean():.2f}, '
          f'typical gap = {np.abs(means - mu).mean():.2f}, biggest gap = {np.abs(means - mu).max():.2f}')
solution.answer: mu = 63.00 and sigma = 12.93. Samples of 2 give 28 possible means with a typical gap of 7.11 (the worst is 19.50). Samples of 5 give 56 means with a typical gap of 3.17 (the worst is 8.40). All sample means average exactly 63.00, so sampling is not biased, and bigger samples land closer to mu.
